title: No. 4 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence) (Jay)
paragraphs: My last paper gave several reasons why the safety of the people would be best secured by union against the danger that may come from JUST causes of war given to other nations. Those reasons show that such causes would not only be given more rarely, but would also be more easily settled, by a national government than by either the State governments or the proposed small confederacies.

But the safety of the people of America against dangers from FOREIGN force depends not only on their refraining from giving JUST causes of war to other nations, but also on placing and keeping themselves in a position that does not INVITE hostility or insult. For it hardly needs to be said that there are PRETENDED as well as just causes of war.

It is too true, however shameful to human nature, that nations in general will make war whenever they see a prospect of gaining anything by it. Indeed, absolute monarchs will often make war when their nations stand to gain nothing—pursuing purely personal aims such as thirst for military glory, revenge for personal insults, ambition, or private agreements to enrich or support their particular families or partisans. These and various other motives, which affect only the mind of the sovereign, often lead him into wars not justified by justice or by the voice and interests of his people. But, apart from these inducements to war—which are more common in absolute monarchies, though they well deserve our attention—there are others that affect nations as often as kings, and some of them, on examination, will be found to grow out of our particular situation and circumstances.

With France and Britain we are rivals in the fisheries, and we can supply their markets more cheaply than they can themselves, despite any efforts to prevent it through bounties on their own fish or duties on foreign fish.

With them and with most other European nations we are rivals in shipping and the carrying trade. We will deceive ourselves if we suppose any of them will rejoice to see it flourish. For since our carrying trade cannot grow without to some degree shrinking theirs, it is more in their interest, and will be more their policy, to restrict it than to promote it.

In the trade with China and India, we interfere with more than one nation, since it allows us to share advantages they had largely monopolized, and since we thereby supply ourselves with goods we used to buy from them.

The expansion of our own commerce in our own ships cannot please any nations that hold territories on or near this continent. The cheapness and excellence of our products, combined with our nearness, the enterprise and skill of our merchants and navigators, will give us a greater share in the advantages those territories afford than the wishes or policies of their respective sovereigns will allow.

Spain finds it convenient to close the Mississippi against us on one side, and Britain shuts us out from the Saint Lawrence on the other. Neither will permit the other waters between them and us to become channels for mutual exchange and trade.

The people of America are aware that motives for war may arise from these circumstances, as well as from others not yet so obvious; and that whenever such motives find the right time and opportunity, pretexts to color and justify them will not be lacking. Wisely, therefore, do they consider union and a good national government as necessary to put and keep them in SUCH A SITUATION as will tend to repress and discourage war rather than INVITE it. That situation consists in the best possible state of defense, and necessarily depends on the government, the arms, and the resources of the country.

Since the safety of the whole is the interest of the whole, and cannot be provided for without government, whether one or several or many, let us inquire whether one good government is not, with respect to the matter at hand, more capable than any other given number whatever.

One government can collect and use the talents and experience of the ablest men, wherever in the Union they may be found. It can act on uniform principles of policy. It can harmonize, integrate, and protect its various parts and members, and extend the benefit of its foresight and precautions to each. In forming treaties, it will consider the interest of the whole and the particular interests of the parts as connected with that of the whole. It can apply the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any particular part, and do so more easily and quickly than State governments or separate confederacies could possibly do, given their lack of coordination and unity. It can place the militia under one plan of discipline, and by putting their officers in proper subordination to the Chief Magistrate, will, in effect, consolidate them into one corps, making them more effective than if divided into thirteen, or into three or four distinct, independent companies.

What would the militia of Britain be if the English militia obeyed the government of England, the Scottish militia obeyed the government of Scotland, and the Welsh militia obeyed the government of Wales? Suppose an invasion: would those three governments, even if they agreed at all, be able with all their forces to act against the enemy as effectively as the single government of Great Britain?

We have heard much of the fleets of Britain, and the time may come, if we are wise, when the fleets of America may attract attention. But if one national government had not so regulated the navigation of Britain as to make it a nursery for seamen—if one national government had not summoned all the national means and materials for forming fleets—their power and their thunder would never have been celebrated. Let England have its navigation and fleet; let Scotland have its navigation and fleet; let Wales have its navigation and fleet; let Ireland have its navigation and fleet; let those four constituent parts of the British empire be under four independent governments, and it is easy to see how soon each would shrink into comparative insignificance.

Apply these facts to our own case. Leave America divided into thirteen, or, if you prefer, into three or four independent governments—what armies could they raise and pay? What fleets could they ever hope to have? If one were attacked, would the others fly to its rescue and spend their blood and money in its defense? Would there be no danger of their being flattered into neutrality by its plausible promises, or seduced by too great a love of peace into refusing to risk their tranquility and present safety for the sake of neighbors of whom they have perhaps been jealous, and whose importance they are content to see diminished? Such conduct would not be wise, but it would be natural. The history of the states of Greece, and of other countries, abounds with such examples, and it is not unlikely that what has so often happened would, under similar circumstances, happen again.

But suppose they were willing to help the invaded State or confederacy. How, when, and in what proportion would aid in men and money be provided? Who would command the allied armies, and from which of them would he take his orders? Who would settle the terms of peace, and in case of disputes what umpire would decide between them and force compliance? Various difficulties and inconveniences would be inseparable from such a situation; whereas one government, watching over the general and common interests, and combining and directing the powers and resources of the whole, would be free of all these embarrassments and would do far more for the safety of the people.

But whatever our situation—whether firmly united under one national government, or split into a number of confederacies—it is certain that foreign nations will know and view it exactly as it is, and will act toward us accordingly. If they see that our national government is effective and well administered, our trade prudently regulated, our militia properly organized and disciplined, our resources and finances discreetly managed, our credit re-established, our people free, content, and united, they will be far more inclined to cultivate our friendship than to provoke our resentment. If, on the other hand, they find us either lacking an effective government (each State doing right or wrong as its rulers find convenient), or split into three or four independent and probably discordant republics or confederacies—one inclining to Britain, another to France, and a third to Spain, and perhaps played off against one another by all three—what a poor, pitiful figure will America cut in their eyes! How exposed she would become not only to their contempt but to their abuse, and how soon would dear-bought experience proclaim that when a people or family so divides, it never fails to be against itself.
